p: Timothy is named beside Paul, but the letter speaks as 'I' almost everywhere.
b: Timothy joined Paul at Lystra on the journey that brought the missionaries to Philippi (Acts 16:1-3), and Acts names him again with Silas at Berea soon after (Acts 17:14), so he probably knew the church from its start. He is named as co-sender, as in 2 Corinthians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters and Philemon, yet from 1:3 on the voice is Paul's 'I', and in 2:19-23 Paul speaks about Timothy in the third person. Most readers take Timothy as a co-sender known to the church, perhaps also the scribe, rather than a co-author. The two are called 'slaves' together, and the letter will later describe Timothy serving Paul 'like a child beside his father' (2:22).

p: The Greek doulos means a slave. Paul uses no title of rank here, only ownership by Christ.
b: Douloi are slaves, people owned by a master. Many English Bibles soften it to 'servants'; the site keeps 'slave' as in Romans 1:1 and Galatians 1:10. Paul drops his usual title 'apostle' in this letter, perhaps because he is writing to friends and not defending his authority. The word prepares for 2:7, where Christ takes 'a slave's form': the senders bear the same title as the one whose way of thinking the letter asks the church to share. In a Roman colony with many slaves, the word would not sound pious; it would sound low. Paul uses slavery here as a picture of belonging wholly to Christ; the letter says nothing for or against the institution itself (see the topic page on slavery).

p: 'Saints' here means all the believers, God's holy people, not a special few.
b: Hagioi means 'holy ones', people set apart for God. In the Old Testament the word belongs to Israel (Exodus 19:6 calls Israel a holy nation). Paul gives it to a mostly Gentile church in a Roman colony. The letter ends the same way: 'Give my greeting to every one of the saints in Christ Jesus' (4:21). The later sense of a saint as an especially holy person who has died is not what the word means here.

t: Overseers and deacons: the first named church officers
p: The only greeting in Paul's letters that names church officers. Both words are plural.
b: Episkopoi are 'overseers' (the word behind English 'bishop') and diakonoi 'servants' or 'helpers' (the word behind 'deacon'). The Greek has no article: 'with overseers and deacons'. Two things stand out. Philippi has several overseers in one church, and Acts 20:17 and 20:28 call the same leaders 'elders' and 'overseers'. And the words were ordinary Greek titles for supervisors and helpers in clubs and towns before they became church offices. Readers differ on how settled these offices already were: some see the beginning of the later order of bishop, priest and deacon; others see local leaders, perhaps those who gathered the gift Paul thanks them for (4:10-18). See the card on this chapter.

p: Paul's greeting joins the Greek word for 'greetings' with the Jewish wish of peace.
b: An ordinary Greek letter opened with chairein, 'greetings'. Paul writes charis, 'grace', a word from the same root, and adds 'peace', the Jewish shalom. The same greeting stands in Romans 1:7, 1 Corinthians 1:3 and Ephesians 1:2. Grace and peace come from 'God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ' together, one preposition for both, which already places Jesus beside God as the source of blessing.

a: Each time you come to mind
t: My memory of you, or your memory of me?
p: The Greek can mean Paul's remembering them or their remembering him, by their gifts.
orig: ἐπὶ πάσῃ τῇ μνείᾳ ὑμῶν (epi pase te mneia hymon)
b: Epi pase te mneia hymon is literally 'upon all the remembrance of you'. The usual reading takes 'of you' as what Paul remembers: he thanks God every time he thinks of them. Another reading takes 'you' as the ones remembering: Paul thanks God for all their remembrance of him, that is, their gifts and care (4:10, 'your thinking of me'). The Plain English Translation follows the usual reading, which matches the prayers 'for you all' in 1:4.

p: Joy and rejoicing come up about sixteen times in four chapters. Paul writes it from prison.
b: The noun chara 'joy' and the verb chairo 'rejoice', with synchairo 'rejoice together', run through the whole letter (1:4, 18, 25; 2:2, 17-18, 28-29; 3:1; 4:1, 4, 10). The Plain English Translation keeps 'joy' and 'rejoice' each time so the reader can follow the thread. The joy is not a mood that ignores trouble: Paul is in chains, rivals preach against him, a friend nearly died, and the church faces opponents. Joy here is gladness at what God is doing in the middle of it. Many readers call Philippians 'the letter of joy' for that reason.

t: Koinonia: partners in the good news
p: The Greek koinonia is a shared stake: partners in a business or a common cause.
b: Koinonia is often translated 'fellowship', but the word family also names partners in a shared undertaking: in Luke 5:10 James and John 'were in business with Simon' (koinonoi). That fits Philippians, where it returns in 1:7 ('you all have a share with me'), 2:1 ('fellowship' of the Spirit), 3:10 ('share his sufferings') and especially 4:14-15, where the church 'went into partnership' with Paul 'in a matter of giving and receiving'. The partnership is in 'the good news' (to euangelion), the message of Christ, which the Plain English Translation calls 'the good news' throughout. The Philippians were partners from 'the first day' (Acts 16:13-15).

a: the one who started a good work in you
t: Who started the good work, and what is it?
p: God began it; the 'good work' may be their faith itself, or their partnership in the gospel.
b: The one who began is God (compare 2:13, 'the one at work in you is God'). The verb enarchomai 'begin' and epiteleo 'complete' are paired in Galatians 3:3 as well. Readers differ on the 'good work': God's saving work in each believer, which he will finish (a verse much used for the assurance of salvation), or more narrowly the church's partnership in the good news (1:5), which God will keep going. 'In you' can also mean 'among you', the whole church. The two readings are not far apart: the work God started at Lydia's riverside meeting is the church itself.

p: Paul takes the prophets' 'day of the LORD' and names it after Christ.
b: The prophets spoke of 'the day of the LORD', when God would come to judge and to set things right. Paul's letters speak of 'the day of Christ' (1:10; 2:16) and 'the day of our Lord Jesus Christ' (1 Corinthians 1:8). The change of name puts Jesus where the prophets put Israel's God. For Paul the day is the end of the race (2:16; 3:14), when the work God began will be finished.

a: since I carry you in my heart
t: I have you in my heart, or you have me in yours?
p: The Greek can mean 'I hold you in my heart' or 'you hold me in your heart'.
b: The Greek infinitive phrase has two accusatives, me 'me' and hymas 'you', and either can be the subject. 'Because I have you in my heart' is the usual reading, since 'me' comes first and the verse is about Paul's feelings. 'Because you have me in your heart' is also good Greek and fits the church's gifts and prayers for him. The Plain English Translation follows the usual reading.
orig: διὰ τὸ ἔχειν με ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ ὑμᾶς

p: Paul is a prisoner awaiting a hearing; 'defense' is the word for a reply in court.
b: Paul speaks of his 'chains' four times in this chapter (1:7, 13, 14, 16). In Rome, Acts says, Paul lived under guard with a soldier and spoke of 'this chain' (Acts 28:16, 20). Apologia 'defense' is the legal reply to a charge, and bebaiosis means 'making firm, confirming'. Paul pictures his coming hearing as a trial of the good news itself, and says the Philippians share in that grace with him. Where he was held is debated (see the book page).

a: the tender heart of Christ Jesus
t: Splanchna: the heart in the gut
p: The Greek word means the inner organs, where Greeks felt deep emotion.
b: Splanchna means the inward parts, the heart, lungs and liver. Greek speakers placed strong feeling there as English speakers place it in the 'heart'. Paul loves the Philippians not only with his own feelings but with Christ's: his love is Christ loving them through him. The same word comes back in 2:1, 'warmth of heart', and in Philemon 7, 12, 20.

p: The Greek can mean 'approve what is excellent' or 'tell apart things that differ'.
b: Dokimazein ta diapheronta: dokimazo is to test metal and approve it, and ta diapheronta can mean 'the things that differ' or 'the things that stand out'. So Paul asks either for the skill to sort right from wrong, or for the skill to see what really matters and choose it. The same phrase is in Romans 2:18. The Plain English Translation takes the second sense, which includes the first.

p: The Greek 'fruit of righteousness' may be fruit that righteousness produces, or fruit that is righteousness.
b: Karpos dikaiosynes is singular in the critical text ('fruit'); the Byzantine text and the KJV have the plural 'fruits'. The genitive can mean the fruit that comes from being made right with God, or the fruit that consists of right living. The phrase echoes Amos 6:12 and Proverbs 11:30 in the Greek. Either way, Paul says it comes 'through Jesus Christ' and ends in God's glory, not the church's.

p: The Greek plural 'brothers' addresses the whole church, women included.
b: Adelphoi, 'brothers', was the normal Greek way to address a mixed group, as 'guys' can be today. The site writes 'brothers' as in Romans and Acts, with the gloss 'brothers and sisters'. In this church the point is plain: the first believer was Lydia (Acts 16:14-15), and Paul names Euodia and Syntyche as his co-workers (4:2-3).

p: The word can mean the Praetorian Guard in Rome or a governor's palace in a province.
b: Praitorion is a Latin word in Greek letters. In Rome it could mean the Praetorian Guard, the emperor's soldiers, or their camp. In the provinces it was the governor's residence: Acts says Paul was 'held under guard in Herod's Praetorium' at Caesarea (Acts 23:35), and the Gospels use it for Pilate's headquarters. So the word fits a Roman imprisonment (the whole guard has heard why Paul is chained) and also Caesarea or another governor's seat such as Ephesus. 'The whole praetorium and everyone else' suggests people, not a building.

t: Brothers in the Lord, or confident in the Lord?
p: 'In the Lord' can go with 'the brothers' or with 'gained confidence'.
b: The Greek reads 'most of the brothers in the Lord trusting my chains'. 'In the Lord' may describe the brothers (fellow believers) or the source of their new confidence. The Plain English Translation joins it to 'confidence', the more common reading, since 'brothers' alone already means believers.

p: Paul does not name them. They preach the true Christ but with bad motives.
b: These preachers are not the false teachers of chapter 3: Paul says their message is Christ and he rejoices in it (1:18). Their fault is motive, envy and rivalry, perhaps a wish to gain from Paul's absence or to make him look weak. The letter gives no names. Suggestions include local leaders who resented Paul, Jewish-Christian missionaries who disagreed with him on the law, or preachers who thought a chained apostle was a disgrace. The point for the Philippians is the contrast with 2:3-4: Paul cares more that Christ is announced than about his own name.

p: Ambition that serves yourself or your faction, rivalry: the opposite of 2:3-4.
b: Eritheia means ambition, self-seeking, rivalry (the lexicons give these senses); Paul lists it among the works of the flesh (Galatians 5:20). It returns in 2:3, 'Do nothing to push yourselves forward', where the Plain English Translation uses the same English. The rivals in Rome or wherever Paul is held show exactly the attitude the church must avoid.

t: Which comes first: ambition or love?
p: The oldest manuscripts give the 'love' sentence first; modern Bibles number it 1:16.
b: This site numbers verses as the KJV does, and the KJV, with the Byzantine text, has the 'selfish ambition' sentence as 1:16 and the 'love' sentence as 1:17. The oldest manuscripts, among them P46, Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, and the critical editions (the SBL text and NA28) have the two sentences the other way round, so most modern Bibles number the 'love' sentence 1:16. The words are the same in both orders. The earlier order answers 1:15 in a crossing pattern: envy and rivalry, good will (1:15); love, ambition (1:16-17). The variant entry on this verse lets you read the lines in that order.

p: Prophasis is a pretext, a cover story; Paul cares only that Christ is announced.
b: Prophasis is an excuse or false front, the opposite of aletheia, truth. Paul's answer is generous but not careless: he does not say false teaching is fine (contrast 3:2 and Galatians 1:8-9), only that a true message preached from mixed motives still does good.

a: this will end in my salvation
p: These words match the Greek of Job 13:16 exactly: 'this will turn out for my salvation'.
b: The Greek touto moi apobesetai eis soterian is word for word the Septuagint of Job 13:16, where Job is sure that God will vindicate him in the end. The site's Plain English Translation of the Hebrew reads 'Even this will turn into my rescue' (Job 13:16). Paul, like Job, is a righteous man on trial. 'Salvation' (soteria) can mean release from prison, vindication at the hearing, or final salvation before God. The next verse ('whether by life or by death') shows Paul does not mean only release: whatever the verdict, God will vindicate him. Many English versions say 'deliverance'; the Plain English Translation keeps 'salvation' so the reader can weigh both senses.

p: A rare phrase: the Spirit belongs to Jesus Christ as well as to God.
b: Paul usually says 'the Spirit of God'. Here, as in Romans 8:9 ('the Spirit of Christ') and Galatians 4:6 ('the Spirit of his Son'), the Spirit is named after Jesus. Epichoregia 'help, supply' is the noun of a verb used for providing what is needed (it is the verb behind 'gives you the Spirit' in Galatians 3:5). The Philippians have supplied Paul's needs (4:18); the Spirit supplies what the trial needs.

p: The citizen's right to speak openly; for a prisoner, courage to speak.
b: Parresia means speaking openly, with nothing held back. The site's term is 'freedom of speech' or 'speak freely' (Acts 4:13; 28:31). A chained man claims it: in court he will speak openly about Christ. 'Not be put to shame' echoes the Psalms' prayers that the one who trusts God will not be disgraced (Psalm 25:2-3).

a: living is Christ and dying is gain
t: Living is Christ, dying is gain
p: Life means Christ, so death cannot rob Paul. It only adds more of him.
b: The two halves are an accounting pair (kerdos 'gain', as in 3:7-8 'profits' and 'loss'). If living is Christ, then death, which brings Paul to Christ (1:23), is gain, not loss. Paul's reason is not escape from trouble but being 'with Christ'. It does not praise suicide: Paul chooses to stay (1:24-25).

t: 'I do not know' or 'I will not tell'?
p: The verb usually means 'make known', so Paul may be refusing to reveal his choice.
b: Everywhere else in Paul's letters, including 4:6 of this one, gnorizo means 'make known, declare' (1 Corinthians 12:3; 15:1; Galatians 1:11). So the clause may mean 'I am not telling'. Many versions render it 'I do not know'. The broken grammar of the verse (the SBL prints a dash) shows Paul thinking aloud.

a: to leave and be with Christ
p: A key text for what happens at death. Paul expects to be with Christ at once.
b: Analysai means to loosen, and so to set off or depart; in Luke 12:36 the same verb is used of a master's return from a wedding feast. Paul expects death to bring him 'with Christ', and calls that 'much, much better' (a doubled comparative). Many readers take this as proof of conscious life with Christ between death and the resurrection (compare 2 Corinthians 5:8). Others note that Paul elsewhere speaks of the dead as 'asleep' and puts his hope in the resurrection at Christ's coming (3:20-21; 1 Thessalonians 4:13-17), and hold that the believer's next conscious moment after death is the resurrection. See the card on this chapter and the topic page.

a: I will stay, and stay alongside
p: Meno and parameno: 'I will remain and remain beside you'.
b: Paul plays on two forms of one verb, meno 'stay' and parameno 'stay on beside'. The Byzantine text and the KJV have symparameno, 'continue with', with no change of sense. He is sure he will survive, though in 2:17 he still speaks of being poured out. The confidence rests on what the church needs (1:24), not on news of his case.

p: Paul uses the verb for public life in a city, in a city proud of its Roman status.
b: Paul does not use his usual verb 'walk' (peripateo) but politeuesthe, 'live as citizens, conduct your public life'. Philippi was a Roman colony, re-founded after the battle of 42 BC, whose people were proud to be Roman (Acts 16:21, 'we, as Romans'). Paul tells them to live as citizens worthy of a different allegiance, the good news of Christ. The theme returns in 3:20, 'we belong to a commonwealth in heaven'. Paul uses the same verb of his own life in Acts 23:1 ('I have lived as a citizen before God').

p: 'Spirit' may be the Holy Spirit or a shared spirit among them.
b: The Greek en heni pneumati can mean 'in one (Holy) Spirit' (as in 1 Corinthians 12:13 and Ephesians 2:18) or 'with one shared spirit'. The pairing with 'with one soul' (mia psyche) suggests the shared attitude; the Plain English Translation uses lower case. 'Fighting side by side' (synathleo) is a word from team athletics and the arena; it returns in 4:3 for Euodia and Syntyche.

p: A rare verb: to be startled, frightened. It is found nowhere else in the New Testament.
b: Ptyromai, 'be startled, be frightened', occurs only here in the New Testament. The 'opponents' are not named. Acts 16:19-24 shows the kind of trouble the church faced from the start: owners of a slave girl, city magistrates, a beating and prison. The Greek is a participle, 'not being startled', still part of what Paul hopes to hear about them (1:27). The church's calm is itself a sign: of ruin to those who oppose God, and of salvation to them.

p: Paul says suffering for Christ is something given, like faith, not a sign of God's absence.
b: The verb echaristhe 'was given as a gift' shares the root of 'grace'. Paul places believing and suffering side by side as gifts. This does not praise pain for its own sake; it says that suffering for Christ joins a person to him (3:10). Some have also misused it to excuse injustice; the letter itself is about suffering that comes from loyalty to Christ, not suffering imposed and left unchallenged.

p: The Philippians saw Paul beaten and jailed in their own city (Acts 16).
b: Agon is an athletic contest or a struggle. The Philippians 'watched' Paul's: he and Silas were stripped, beaten with rods and locked in the stocks in Philippi (Acts 16:22-24; compare 1 Thessalonians 2:2). Now they 'hear' of his present chains. Their own trouble is the same contest, which makes them partners with him again.

a: if the Spirit gives any fellowship
p: Each 'if' assumes the thing is true: since there is encouragement in Christ...
b: The four clauses use ei 'if' with no doubt implied: 'if there is (and there is)'. The list moves from Christ to love to the Spirit to the warmth and pity Christians feel, and the conclusion is 2:2, 'make my joy full'. Koinonia pneumatos may be fellowship that the Spirit creates or a shared life in the Spirit; compare 2 Corinthians 13:14, 'the fellowship of the Holy Spirit'. See the note on 'partnership' at 1:5.

p: Paul's verb 'think, set your mind on' runs through the letter, ten times in four chapters.
b: Phroneo means more than having thoughts: it is a settled way of seeing and caring, a mindset. Paul uses it in 1:7, twice here, in 2:5 (the mind of Christ), twice in 3:15, in 3:19 (those who 'think about earthly things'), in 4:2 (Euodia and Syntyche) and twice in 4:10 (the church 'thinking of me'). The Plain English Translation says 'think' almost every time so the thread is visible (in 3:15 'if you think otherwise' becomes 'if you see something differently'). Unity in Philippians is not everyone holding the same opinion on everything; it is everyone sharing Christ's way of thinking (2:5).

t: Humility, a low word made high
p: Tapeinos means low, of small account. Paul ties the word family together across the letter.
b: Tapeinophrosyne is 'lowliness of mind', humility. Its root tapeinos means low, poor, of small account. Paul ties the word family together across the letter: here the church's 'lowly mind', in 2:8 Christ 'made himself low', in 3:21 'our low state', and in 4:12 Paul knows 'how to live low'. In 2:8 the hymn uses two reflexive verbs, 'he emptied himself' and 'he made himself low': no one forced him, and he was 'obedient' to God. Paul sets that obedience against Adam's disobedience in Romans 5:19: 'the one man obeyed, and the many will be made righteous' (Romans 5:19). Jesus' saying 'anyone who brings himself low will be raised up' (Matthew 23:12) is the pattern of 2:8-9.

a: the way that is also in Christ Jesus
p: Either 'think as Christ thought' or 'think in the way that fits your life in Christ'.
b: The Greek has no verb in the second half: 'think this among you, which also in Christ Jesus'. The example reading supplies 'was': have the attitude Jesus had (most translations; the Byzantine text's 'let this mind be' points the same way). The setting reading supplies 'you have' or 'is fitting': think in the way that belongs to people who are 'in Christ', the church's shared life (some modern scholars, and the Catechism quotes the verse 'which is yours in Christ Jesus', CCC 461). Both readings lead into the hymn; they differ on whether Christ is mainly a model or the ground of a new life. The Plain English Translation keeps the Greek gap open with 'is'.

a: Being in the form of God
p: Morphe is 'form': the shape in which something shows what it is. Readers differ on how much it says.
b: Morphe means form, shape, appearance; in philosophical Greek it could mean the essential form of a thing (the lexicons give both). So readers take 'the form of God' as (1) God's very nature, so that Christ was fully God (Chrysostom: 'If the form of God is perfect God, then the form of a servant is a perfect servant'); (2) God's glory or majesty as it is seen (Calvin: 'The form of God means here his majesty'); (3) a status or role; or (4) the image of God in which Adam was made (James Dunn and Oscar Cullmann see an Adam parallel; Cullmann ties 'form' to the 'image' of Genesis 1:26). The same word in 2:7, 'a slave's form', keeps the two halves matched. Hyparchon 'being' is a present participle: he was already in that form.
orig: ἐν μορφῇ θεοῦ ὑπάρχων (en morphe theou hyparchon)

t: Harpagmos: robbery, a prize, or something to exploit?
p: A rare word found nowhere else in the Bible. Each translation of it is a theological choice.
b: Harpagmos comes from harpazo, 'seize'. Taken actively it means 'robbery' or 'the act of seizing' (KJV 'thought it not robbery to be equal with God': Christ was equal by right). Taken as a thing seized, it is a 'prize', either one he did not have and would not snatch (res rapienda) or one he had and would not cling to (res retinenda). The lexicon of Abbott-Smith says the word's usage favors the active sense, though most interpreters prefer 'prize'. Roy Hoover (1971) argued that in this idiom the word means something to take advantage of; J. C. O'Neill (1988) disputed it. The Plain English Translation follows Hoover's reading: Christ did not use his equality with God for his own advantage. Chrysostom already read it so: he held equality 'not by seizure, but it was natural'.

p: The hymn assumes Christ had equality with God before he became human.
b: To einai isa theo is 'being equal to God'. Most readers take the hymn to say that Christ shared God's status before his human birth: he was 'in the form of God' and did not use that equality for himself. A minority reading, linked to the Adam parallel, says the hymn contrasts Jesus with Adam, who grasped at being 'like God' (Genesis 3:5), without saying that Jesus existed before his birth. Against it, others point to 'emptied himself' and 'coming to be in the likeness of human beings' (2:7), which describe a choice made by someone who was not yet human. See the card on this chapter.

p: The verb gives the word 'kenosis'. Paul does not say what Christ emptied himself of.
b: Kenoo means 'to empty, make empty, make void'. Paul uses it in Romans 4:14 ('faith is emptied') and 1 Corinthians 1:17 ('the cross of Christ would not be made empty'). Here it is reflexive: he emptied himself. The hymn explains how by the next words: 'taking a slave's form, coming to be in the likeness of human beings'. The emptying is the taking, not a list of things removed. Readers have asked what was set aside: the use of divine power, the outward glory, the divine privileges, or (in the nineteenth-century kenotic theories) some divine attributes. Some hear Isaiah 53:12, where the servant 'emptied out his life to the point of death'. See the deep dive on this chapter and the topic page.

p: God's form and a slave's form: the lowest status in Roman society set against the highest.
b: In a Roman colony, a slave was the person with no rights, no honor and no say over his own body. The hymn sets 'the form of God' against 'a slave's form', the top and the bottom of the ancient order. Readers also hear 'the servant of the LORD' of Isaiah 52:13-53:12, who would be 'he will be high and lifted up, / and very exalted' (Isaiah 52:13) after his suffering; the Greek of Isaiah calls him pais, not doulos, so the link is in the story more than in the word. Jesus' own saying, 'He came to serve, and to give his life as a ransom in place of many' (Mark 10:45), makes the same move.

p: Homoioma 'likeness' and schema 'outward shape' do not mean he only seemed human.
b: Homoioma 'likeness' (as in Romans 8:3, 'the likeness of sinful flesh') and in 2:8 schema 'outward shape, bearing' describe how he appeared to others. Some early readers, the Docetists and Marcion's followers, took such words to mean Christ only looked human; Chrysostom answers the Marcionites in his homily on this passage. Most interpreters read the words as stressing that he was truly seen and known as a human being, while remaining who he was. 'Human beings' is plural in Greek: he entered the human race.

a: Found in outward shape as a human being
p: In the Greek editions these words close verse 7; English Bibles begin verse 8 with them.
b: The SBL and NA28 print 'and being found in outward shape as a human being' at the end of 2:7. The KJV numbering, which this site follows, starts 2:8 with them. Nothing in the text changes. The difference matters only for the hymn's layout: some scholars arrange the lines in pairs or stanzas, and where 'found in outward shape' goes affects the pattern.

p: The words break the rhythm. Many scholars think Paul added them to an earlier hymn.
b: 'Death on a cross' (thanatou de staurou) repeats 'death' with a sharp 'yes, even'. Crucifixion was the Roman death for slaves and rebels, a public shame; a citizen of a Roman colony would feel the scandal at once. Ernst Lohmeyer (1928) first set out 2:6-11 as a poem in stanzas, and many who follow him take this line as Paul's own addition, because it spoils the balance of the lines. Others see no need for an earlier hymn at all: some object that the Greek has no meter, and that Paul could write this way himself. Either way, the cross is the lowest point, and in 3:18 Paul names 'enemies of Christ's cross'.

a: That is why God also raised him to the heights
p: The second half of the hymn: God acts. The verb means raised beyond, super-exalted.
b: Hyperypsosen, 'raised beyond, raised to the very top', is found only here in the New Testament. The movement down (2:6-8) by Christ's choice is answered by a movement up by God's act. Readers differ on what 'that is why' means: a reward for obedience, the fitting outcome of who he is, or God showing in public what was always true. Isaiah 52:13 says of the servant that 'he will be high and lifted up, / and very exalted'. The hymn does not name the resurrection: it moves straight from the cross to the throne.

p: Most read 'the name above every name' as 'Lord', God's own title in the Greek Bible; some as 'Jesus'.
b: Most readers take the name given to be not 'Jesus', which he had from birth, but the title the next verse declares: 'Jesus Christ is Lord' (2:11). Others take it to be the name 'Jesus' itself, now honored above all, since 2:10 speaks of bending 'at the name of Jesus'. In the Greek Old Testament Kyrios 'Lord' stands for the divine name YHWH. So God gives Jesus his own name, the name that Isaiah 42:8 says God will share with no one: 'I am the LORD; that is my name. / I will not hand my glory to another' (Isaiah 42:8). The hymn's answer is that giving it to Jesus brings 'glory of God the Father' (2:11), not glory to a rival.

t: Isaiah 45:23: God's oath said of Jesus
p: The words come from Isaiah 45:23, where Israel's God swears that every knee will bend to him.
b: In Isaiah 45 the LORD says 'there is no one else' (Isaiah 45:22) and swears: 'every knee will bend before me; / every tongue will take its oath' (Isaiah 45:23). The hymn applies that oath to Jesus, at whose name every knee bends. Paul quotes the same verse of God in Romans 14:11. Many scholars see in texts like this the earliest Christians including Jesus within the worship of the one God of Israel, while still worshiping one God, since the confession ends 'for the glory of God the Father'. Jewish monotheism is not dropped; it is applied to Jesus. 'At the name of Jesus' is literally 'in the name of Jesus' (en to onomati Iesou): at the naming of him, or in honor of the name he has been given. Whether that name is 'Jesus' or 'Lord' is discussed at 2:9.

a: of those in heaven, on earth and under the earth
t: Heaven, earth and under the earth
p: Every kind of being, angels, humans and the dead or the powers below, bows to Jesus.
b: The three Greek adjectives are plural: heavenly ones, earthly ones, those under the earth. Readers take them as the whole universe of living beings: angels, people, and the dead or underworld powers (Revelation 5:13 has a similar list). Some readers have seen in the verse a hope that all will in the end be reconciled; others read it as acknowledgment by all, willing or not, rather than salvation for all. The verse also answers the many 'lords' of Philippi's world, from the emperor to the gods of the underworld.

p: Isaiah's Hebrew says every tongue will 'take its oath'; Paul's Greek says 'confess'.
b: The Hebrew of Isaiah 45:23 ends 'every tongue will take its oath', and the Greek printed in Swete's Septuagint (Codex Vaticanus) agrees, 'will swear'. Paul has exomologesetai, 'will confess, openly acknowledge', the same verb he uses when he quotes the verse in Romans 14:11. To 'confess' in a court or temple was to declare loyalty in public.

p: One of the earliest Christian confessions, and a rival claim in a world where Caesar was 'lord'.
b: 'Jesus is Lord' is the confession of Romans 10:9 ('confess Jesus as Lord with your mouth') and 1 Corinthians 12:3, perhaps said at baptism. In the Greek Old Testament Kyrios stands for God's name. In the Roman world kyrios was also used of the emperor: Festus calls Nero 'our lord' in Acts 25:26. Readers who stress the imperial setting (see the topic page on ruler worship) hear the hymn as a quiet challenge to Caesar in a colony full of veterans; others think the Old Testament background is the main one. The two are not exclusive.

p: Paul is not telling them to earn salvation; the next verse says God is the one at work.
b: Katergazesthe means to carry out, bring to completion. 'Your own' is plural: the church as a whole is addressed, and the verse follows a call to unity, so some read 'salvation' as the health of the community. Most read it as each believer's life working out the salvation given, 'with fear and trembling' (compare 'Serve the LORD in fear, / and be glad with trembling', Psalm 2:11, and 2 Corinthians 7:15). The reason given is 2:13: God works in them. Wesley's sermon on these verses put it as 'God worketh in you; therefore you can work' and 'therefore you must work'. See the card on this chapter.

a: for the sake of what pleases him
p: The Greek says only 'for the good pleasure': God's good purpose, or good will among them.
b: Hyper tes eudokias has no 'his'. Most take it as God's good pleasure, as in Ephesians 1:5, 9. A few read it as 'for the sake of good will', the church's harmony, which fits the call to unity. The verb 'is at work' (energeo) and 'the doing' (energein) are the same root: God works the willing and the working. Calvinist readers stress that God gives even the will; Arminian and Wesleyan readers stress that he enables it without forcing it.

t: Israel's wilderness, and Moses' song turned around
p: 2:14-15 borrow Israel's wilderness story: its grumbling, and the twisted generation of Deuteronomy 32:5.
b: Deuteronomy 32:5 says of Israel: 'they are not his children, they are a blot, / a warped and twisted generation' (Deuteronomy 32:5). The echo begins in 2:14: gongysmos, 'grumbling, muttering', is the Greek Old Testament's word for Israel's complaints in the desert: God 'has heard your complaints' (Exodus 16:7), 'the complaints the Israelites keep making against me' (Numbers 14:27), and Paul uses the same story as a warning in 1 Corinthians 10:10. The Greek of Deuteronomy 32:5 reads tekna mometa, genea skolia kai diestrammene, 'blemished children, a warped and twisted generation'. Paul turns it around: the church are God's children 'with no flaw' (amoma), living in the middle of such a generation. He does not say the Jewish people are that generation; the people around the Philippians were mostly Gentiles. Jesus uses similar words in Matthew 17:17.
r: Deuteronomy 32:5; Exodus 16:7; Numbers 14:27; 1 Corinthians 10:10; Matthew 17:17; Acts 2:40

t: Lights like the stars in Daniel
p: The word phosteres is used of the sun, moon and stars, and of the wise in Daniel 12:3.
b: Phosteres are 'lights, luminaries', the word the Greek of Genesis 1:14-16 uses for the sun and moon. In the Old Greek of Daniel 12:3 the wise 'will shine like the lights of heaven' (hos phosteres tou ouranou); the site's Plain English Translation of the Hebrew says 'Those with insight will gleam / like the gleam of the dome of the sky' (Daniel 12:3). The believers already shine now, before the resurrection Daniel speaks of. Matthew 5:14, 'You are the light of the world', is close in thought.

a: holding out the word of life
p: The verb can mean offering the word to others or holding firmly to it.
b: Epechontes can mean 'holding out, offering' (as one holds out food) or 'holding fast'. The first fits 'lights in the world', a church that shows and offers the message. The second fits the warnings about standing firm. Many modern translations choose 'holding firmly'; the Plain English Translation chooses 'holding out', but both are possible.

a: did not work hard for nothing
p: Paul pictures his work as a race and borrows the servant's words in Isaiah 49:4.
b: Paul often speaks of his mission as running (Galatians 2:2; 1 Corinthians 9:24-26). 'Work hard for nothing' echoes the servant of the LORD: 'I have worked hard for nothing' (Isaiah 49:4), in Greek kenos ekopiasa, the same verb kopiao. The servant's complaint ends in trust that his reward is with God; Paul expects his reward 'on the day of Christ' to be the Philippians themselves (4:1).

a: poured out as a drink offering
p: In Israel's worship and in Greek rites, wine was poured out with a sacrifice.
b: Spendomai 'I am poured out as a drink offering'. The Law commanded wine poured out with the burnt offerings: 'present half a hin of wine for the drink offering' (Numbers 15:10; compare Numbers 28:7). Greek and Roman worship also poured libations, so every reader in Philippi would know the picture. The Philippians' faith is the sacrifice; Paul's life, perhaps his death, is the wine poured over it. 2 Timothy 4:6 uses the same verb of Paul's coming death. Paul turns their life into worship and his into its finishing touch. 'Priestly service' (leitourgia) is the word family the Greek Old Testament uses for the Levites' service at the tabernacle (Numbers 1:50; 3:6), and Luke for Zechariah's priestly duty (Luke 1:23). Paul uses it three times in this chapter: their 'priestly service' (2:17), Epaphroditus as their leitourgos sent to serve his needs (2:25), and the 'service' they sent (2:30). Giving to Paul is worship.
r: Numbers 15:5-10; Numbers 28:7; Numbers 1:50; Luke 1:23; 2 Timothy 4:6; Romans 12:1; Romans 15:16; 2:25; 2:30

p: Timothy probably knew Philippi from the founding journey; Paul plans to send him as his own eyes.
b: Timothy joined Paul at Lystra just before the journey that reached Philippi (Acts 16:1-3); Acts does not name him in Philippi itself, but names him with Silas at Berea soon after (Acts 17:14), and later sends him into Macedonia (Acts 19:22). Paul's praise in 2:20-22 is a letter of recommendation inside the letter: Timothy will come with Paul's authority. The plan to send him 'the moment I can see what is going to happen to me' (2:23) shows that Paul's case is still undecided.

a: All the others are after what is theirs
p: A strong complaint. Paul does not say who: co-workers nearby, or the rival preachers of 1:15-17.
b: The sentence echoes 2:4: they look after 'what is theirs'. Paul may mean the people available to send, who were unwilling to make the journey, or more broadly the preachers with mixed motives of 1:15-17. Some readers find the words hard to square with Epaphroditus (2:25) and the 'brothers with me' (4:21), and take 'all' as an exaggeration of a moment's frustration. The point for Philippi is Timothy's likeness to Christ, who did not look after his own interests (2:4-7).

p: He carried the Philippians' gift to Paul and probably carried this letter home.
b: Epaphroditus is known only from this letter (2:25-30; 4:18). His name is formed from Aphrodite, the goddess of love, which suggests a Gentile family. The church sent him with money and to stay and help Paul (4:18). He fell gravely ill. Paul now sends him back, and the way he praises him ('hold people of his kind in honor', 2:29) seems meant to protect him from any charge that he came home early.

p: The Greek is apostolos: 'one who is sent'. Here it means the church's envoy, not an apostle of Christ.
b: Apostolos is used here in its plain sense, a person sent with a task, as in 2 Corinthians 8:23 ('messengers of the churches'). The site's term renders such uses 'messenger'. The pairing with leitourgos 'one who serves' (a word with a sacred ring, see the note at 2:17, though the Plain English Translation says simply 'serve') gives Epaphroditus a dignified role: he is the church's representative.

a: nearly to the point of death
t: Why was Epaphroditus not healed at once?
p: Paul worked miracles in Acts, yet here a friend nearly dies, and Paul credits God's mercy.
b: Paul says nothing of healing powers. He speaks of illness 'nearly to the point of death', of grief, and of mercy. Readers have used this verse, with 2 Timothy 4:20 (Trophimus left sick), in debates over whether healing is always God's will. Some take it as a sign that gifts of healing were already rare; others answer that Paul never says healing was impossible, only that God showed mercy in his own way. The passage itself is about friendship and sorrow more than doctrine.

t: 'Finally' in the middle of the letter
p: Paul says 'finally' at 3:1, then writes two more chapters. Some scholars see a seam here.
b: To loipon can mean 'finally' or simply 'as for the rest, so then'. After it the tone changes sharply at 3:2, from 'rejoice' to 'look out for the dogs'. Many scholars since the nineteenth century have taken this as the join between two or three letters that were later combined: one common proposal puts 4:10-20 as a thank-you note, 1:1-3:1 as a second letter and 3:2-4:1 as a third (Philip Sellew and others). Others defend one letter: to loipon often means 'so then' in the middle of an argument (1 Thessalonians 4:1), and the themes of chapter 3 (the mind, suffering, Christ's form, citizenship) repeat chapters 1 and 2. 'The same things' may point back to warnings given earlier or ahead to what follows. See the book page.

p: A harsh insult. The most common reading: Paul turns a word used of Gentiles back on teachers who demanded circumcision.
b: In the Bible dogs are scavengers and unclean: Jesus speaks of 'the little dogs' in a saying about Gentiles (Matthew 15:26), and Revelation 22:15 puts 'the dogs' outside the city. The most common reading is that Paul turns the insult around: the Jewish-Christian teachers who insisted that Gentile believers be circumcised are the real outsiders. Others think of local Jews, pagan cults, Cynic philosophers (whose name means 'doglike') or Christian libertines (see the chapter page). The verse has been turned against Jews. John Chrysostom, preaching on it, called the 'dogs' Jews who 'preached both Christianity and Judaism at the same time', and said that 'once the Gentiles were called dogs, but now the Jews' (Homily 10). Paul's own words do not support that use: in the next verses he counts himself a Hebrew whose parents were Hebrews, of the tribe of Benjamin (3:4-6), and his target is people who would make Gentiles keep the Law to belong, not the Jewish people.

p: Peritome is circumcision; katatome is 'cutting up, mutilation'. Paul mocks by a play on words.
b: Paul sets katatome, 'mutilation, cutting', against peritome, 'circumcision', in 3:3. The Greek Old Testament uses the verb katatemno for cuts forbidden in the Law (compare Leviticus 21:5, priests must not 'make cuts in their bodies'). So Paul says that circumcision demanded of Gentiles as a condition of belonging is no longer the covenant sign but a cutting with no meaning. Galatians 5:12 is still rougher. Paul is not rejecting circumcision for Jews: he lists his own in 3:5.

p: Paul claims Israel's covenant sign for all who worship by the Spirit, Jews and Gentiles.
b: Circumcision was the sign of the covenant with Abraham (Genesis 17). The prophets already spoke of a circumcised heart (Deuteronomy 30:6; Jeremiah 4:4), and Paul says in Romans 2:29 that 'circumcision is of the heart'. Here 'we' includes Gentile believers. Supersessionist readings take the verse to mean the church has replaced Israel; many recent readers answer that Paul is defining who belongs to God's people in Christ without denying Israel's calling (Romans 9:4-5; 11:29). Paul still counts his own circumcision as real (3:5).
r: Genesis 17:10-12; Deuteronomy 30:6; Jeremiah 4:4; Romans 2:28-29; Romans 9:4-5; Galatians 6:15

a: we take pride in Christ Jesus
p: Kauchaomai is 'boast': Paul's boast moves from his record to Christ.
b: The verb kauchaomai is 'boast, take pride'. In 1:26 and 2:16 Paul uses its noun for proper pride in what God has done. Here the contrast is with putting confidence 'in the flesh', which in this chapter means human pedigree and achievement: the list in 3:5-6. Compare Galatians 6:14, 'may I never boast in anything but the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ' (Galatians 6:14).

a: I was circumcised when I was eight days old
p: Seven marks of status: four came with his birth, three with how he lived.
b: Paul lists what made him a model Jew. From his birth: circumcision on the eighth day as the Law required (Genesis 17:12; Leviticus 12:3), so not a convert; the nation of Israel; the tribe of Benjamin, which gave Israel its first king, Saul, Paul's own Hebrew name (Acts 13:21; Romans 11:1); 'a Hebrew whose parents were Hebrews' (literally 'a Hebrew of Hebrews'). From his own life: a Pharisee in his practice of the Law (Acts 23:6); zeal shown in persecuting the church; and a blameless record in the righteousness the Law described. Compare 2 Corinthians 11:22 and Galatians 1:13-14.
r: Genesis 17:12; Leviticus 12:3; Romans 11:1; Acts 13:21; Acts 23:6; 2 Corinthians 11:22; Galatians 1:13-14

a: a Hebrew whose parents were Hebrews
p: Probably: born to Hebrew parents, and perhaps keeping the Hebrew or Aramaic language at home.
b: The Greek Hebraios ex Hebraion is 'a Hebrew from Hebrews'. It can mean pure descent, or, since Acts distinguishes 'Hebrews' from Greek-speaking 'Hellenists' (Acts 6:1), a Jew of a family that kept the ancestral language and customs even outside the land of Israel (Paul was born in Tarsus, Acts 22:3). Both are claims of deep Jewish belonging.

p: The Pharisees were a lay movement that taught a careful keeping of the Law in daily life.
b: The Pharisees were known for exact interpretation of the Law and for traditions of the elders (Mark 7:3; Acts 22:3 'schooled in every detail of our ancestral law'). Paul says 'I am a Pharisee' at his hearing (Acts 23:6). Here he speaks in the past: as to the Law, he was one. He does not say the Pharisees were wrong to love the Law; he says he no longer counts his standing among them as gain.

p: Zeal for God in Paul's tradition could mean violence against those who broke faith (Phinehas).
b: Zeal (zelos) recalls Phinehas, whose 'zeal' for God stopped a plague (Numbers 25:11-13). Paul admits that his zeal made him persecute the church (1 Corinthians 15:9; Galatians 1:13; Acts 9:1). He names it as his credential once, now as loss. In Romans 10:2 he says the same of others: 'they have zeal for God, but it does not go along with knowledge' (Romans 10:2). 'Persecute' (dioko) is the verb he will use in 3:12 and 3:14 for running after the prize.

p: Paul says he kept the Law without fault. This challenges the idea that he felt crushed by guilt.
b: Amemptos 'blameless' means no one could fault his practice, which included the Law's sacrifices for sin. Readers in the line of Krister Stendahl's essay 'The Apostle Paul and the Introspective Conscience of the West' (1963), which argued that the usual Lutheran picture of Paul did not match his own statements, point to this verse: Paul shows no troubled conscience about his past. E. P. Sanders' Paul and Palestinian Judaism (1977) argued that the Judaism of Paul's day was not a religion of earning salvation by works. Others reply that Paul means outward observance, judged by human standards, and that Romans 7 and 3:9 still show that this righteousness could not save. See the topic page on the New Perspective.

p: A crude word: refuse, especially dung. Polite translations soften it.
b: Skybala means refuse, especially dung (the lexicon of Abbott-Smith gives both). The KJV has 'dung'; many modern versions 'rubbish' or 'garbage'. The word is meant to shock. Paul is not calling the Law or Israel's heritage filth; the Law is 'holy' (Romans 7:12). He is saying that, compared with knowing Christ, any status he could claim is worth nothing to him.

p: Paul contrasts a righteousness 'from the law' with one 'from God', received by faith.
b: The contrast is between 'my own righteousness, from the law' and 'the righteousness from God'. In the Reformation reading (Luther, Calvin, the confessions) Paul means a righteousness earned by doing the Law against one given by God and counted to the believer. In the New Perspective reading, 'my own' means the righteousness that marked him out as a faithful Jew, Israel's covenant badge, against a righteousness open to Jews and Gentiles in Christ. In Catholic teaching the righteousness 'from God' is God's own gift that makes the believer truly righteous (Trent: 'the justice of God, not that whereby He Himself is just, but that whereby He maketh us just'). Romans 10:3 makes the same contrast. See the card on this chapter.

t: Faith in Christ, or the faithfulness of Christ? (3:9)
p: 'Faith' comes twice in this verse. That repetition is part of the debate over what 'faith of Christ' means.
b: The Greek is dia pisteos Christou, 'through faith of Christ', then epi te pistei, 'based on (the) faith'. The Plain English Translation reads the first as 'faith in Christ', as Romans 3:22 and Galatians 2:16 do on this site. Those who read 'the faithfulness of Christ' point out that the verse would then name two things: Christ's faithful obedience (the hymn's 'obedient all the way to death', 2:8) and the believer's faith that receives it. Those who read 'faith in Christ' answer that Paul often repeats himself for emphasis, and that 'based on faith' explains the first phrase. Both sides cite this verse; it does not settle the question alone. See the variant entry and the topic page.
orig: διὰ πίστεως Χριστοῦ ... ἐπὶ τῇ πίστει

p: The order is surprising: resurrection power first, then sharing his sufferings.
b: Paul puts 'the power of his rising' before 'what it is to share his sufferings' (koinonia again, see 1:5). The power of the risen Christ is what makes it possible to share his sufferings now. 'Taking on the form of his death' (symmorphizomenos) uses the root of morphe, 'form' (2:6-7): as Christ took a slave's form and died, Paul is shaped to that death. In 3:21 the same root returns for the body that will share 'the form of his body of glory'.

t: Was Paul unsure of the resurrection?
p: 'If somehow' sounds doubtful. Most read it as humility about the way, not doubt about the goal.
b: Ei pos 'if somehow' can express hope with uncertainty. Some readers take it as genuine uncertainty about his own final faithfulness (a text cited in debates over whether believers can fall away); others as uncertainty about how he will reach it, by death or by being alive at Christ's coming; most as humble hope that does not presume. 'Out from among the dead' (exanastasis ten ek nekron) uses a rare compound found only here in the New Testament, which stresses rising out of the company of the dead.
orig: εἴ πως καταντήσω εἰς τὴν ἐξανάστασιν

a: I do not mean that I have already got it
p: Paul denies he is already 'perfect', then calls the mature 'perfect' in 3:15. A deliberate play?
b: Teteleiomai 'I have been made perfect, brought to the goal'. In 3:15 he says 'those of us who are mature' (teleioi, the same root). Many think Paul is answering people who claimed to have arrived already: he has not, and the truly mature know they have not. The verse is the text of Wesley's sermon 'Christian Perfection', which argues that Christians are not perfect in knowledge or free from mistakes and temptation, yet can be perfect in love. The verb katalambano, 'seize, catch hold of', runs through 3:12-13: Paul has not yet 'caught hold of' the goal, but he chases it because Christ 'caught hold of' him, on the Damascus road (Acts 9:3-6); eph' ho can mean 'because' or 'that for which'. In 3:15 'those of us who are mature' (teleioi) are, with a touch of irony, the ones who know they have not arrived, and 'God will show you that too' is a gentle way to end a sharp argument. See the card on this chapter.
r: 3:15; Acts 9:3-6; 1 Corinthians 2:6; 1 Corinthians 9:24; Hebrews 12:23; 1 Corinthians 13:10; Matthew 5:48

t: The prize of the upward call
p: Language from the games: the runner straining for the mark and the prize.
b: Skopos is the mark a runner fixes his eyes on; brabeion is the victor's prize, the same word as in 1 Corinthians 9:24 ('only one gets the prize'). 'The upward call' may be God's summons to come up and receive the prize, as a winner was called up to the stand, or God's call that comes from above. Paul's picture is of a runner who does not look back (3:13), unlike the opponents who glory in their past record.

p: Paul tells them to copy him. It sounds proud, but the model is a life shaped by the cross.
b: Symmimetai is 'fellow imitators': copy me, all together. Ancient teachers taught by example, and Paul often asks churches to imitate him (1 Corinthians 4:16; 11:1, 'as I imitate Christ'). The example he gives in this letter is giving up status (3:7-8), like Christ (2:6-8), and he points them to others who live this way (Timothy, Epaphroditus). Some modern readers worry that such appeals concentrate power in the leader; others answer that Paul's model is self-emptying, not control.

p: Paul weeps over them. Readers differ on whether they are the same people as the 'dogs' of 3:2.
b: Paul calls them 'many' and says they 'walk', so they seem to be people who claim to follow Christ. Readings: the same circumcision party as 3:2, who avoid the shame of the cross by keeping to the safe status of the Law (Galatians 6:12); Christians who turned freedom into indulgence ('their god is the belly'); or people who avoid suffering for Christ. Paul's tears are worth noting: he grieves rather than gloats.

p: Gluttons and libertines, or people centered on food laws and circumcision?
b: 'The belly' (koilia) can mean appetite, as in Romans 16:18 ('They serve their own bellies'). So many readers see self-indulgent people. Others think of teachers fixed on food laws, and read 'what should shame them' as a coarse reference to circumcision, the 'flesh' of 3:3-4. A third reading takes 'shame' as the biblical sense of disgrace before God at the judgment. The verse ends with the key word of the letter: 'their thinking' (phroneo) is on earthly things.

a: we belong to a commonwealth in heaven
t: Citizens of heaven in a Roman colony
p: Politeuma: citizenship, or the community of citizens. Philippi was a colony of Rome far from Rome.
b: Politeuma means citizenship or a commonwealth, a community of citizens (both senses are in the lexicons). Philippi was a Roman colony whose citizens were enrolled as Romans though they lived far from Rome (Acts 16:12, 21). Paul says the church's true city is in heaven, and from there they await a 'Savior' and 'Lord', titles also given to emperors. The point is not that believers will leave earth for heaven; it is that their ruler will come from heaven to transform their bodies (3:21). See 1:27 for the verb.
orig: ἡμῶν γὰρ τὸ πολίτευμα ἐν οὐρανοῖς ὑπάρχει

p: Soter, 'savior, rescuer'. Among Paul's undisputed letters, only here is Jesus called Savior.
b: Soter is used of God in the Greek Old Testament and, in the Roman world, of rulers and gods. Among the letters almost all scholars agree Paul wrote, this is the only place he calls Jesus 'Savior'; Ephesians 5:23 has it too, and the title is common in the Pastoral Letters (Titus 2:13; 2 Timothy 1:10). Set beside 'Lord', it is a claim about who truly protects the city.

p: Christ will change the body's outward shape to share his glorious form: change, not a new body from nothing.
b: Metaschematizo 'change the outward shape' uses the root of schema (2:8), and symmorphon 'sharing the form' the root of morphe (2:6-7). As Christ took the outward shape of a human being and a slave's form, so he will reshape 'the body we have in our low state' into the form of 'his body of glory'. 1 Corinthians 15:43, 51-53 says the same in other words. The verse supports the reading that resurrection is bodily, and that the same person is raised, changed. Readers differ on how much continuity there is between the present and the raised body.

a: to put all things under himself
p: An echo of Psalm 8:6, which Paul also uses in 1 Corinthians 15:27.
b: Psalm 8:6 says of humankind: 'everything you have placed beneath his feet' (Psalm 8:6). Paul applies it to Christ in 1 Corinthians 15:27 ('he put all things under his feet'). Here the power that will subject all things is the same power that will transform the believers' bodies. The line also recalls the hymn's every knee bending (2:10).

p: Two women co-workers in conflict. Paul names them, urges both equally, and praises their work.
b: Paul writes 'I appeal' to each in turn, not taking sides. Their names are Greek (Syntyche means 'fortunate'). He does not say what they disagreed about. He asks them to 'think the same way in the Lord', the letter's key verb (2:2, 5). That their quarrel is named in a letter read to the whole church shows how much they mattered: Chrysostom thought they seemed to be 'the chief of the Church which was there'. Richard Fellows and Alistair Stewart argue that they were householders and patrons of the church, which in Philippi began in Lydia's house (Acts 16:15, 40). In 4:3 Paul says they 'fought at my side', the word of 1:27 (synathleo) for the whole church's struggle for the faith, and places them with Clement and his 'fellow workers' (synergoi), the term he uses for Prisca and Aquila, Timothy and Titus (Romans 16:3, 21; 2 Corinthians 8:23). How far this shows women leading or teaching in Paul's churches is debated: some see clear evidence for women's leadership, others active partnership short of the office of overseer. See the topic page on women in church leadership and the cards at Romans 16:1-7 and 1 Timothy 2.
r: 4:3; 2:2; 2:5; 1:27; Acts 16:15; Acts 16:40; Romans 16:1-7; Romans 16:21; 2 Corinthians 8:23; 1 Timothy 2:11-15

p: A partner under one yoke. Paul does not give a name, unless 'Syzygos' is the name.
b: Syzygos is 'yoke-partner', one of two animals under one yoke. Proposals: (1) a proper name, 'Syzygus', with a pun: 'true to your name' (the lexicon of Abbott-Smith thinks this probable); (2) Epaphroditus, who carried the letter; (3) Timothy, Silas or Luke; (4) not one person but the Philippian church addressed as a whole (Richard Fellows and Alistair Stewart). Clement of Alexandria, as Eusebius reports him, thought Paul greeted his wife in one of his letters, and some applied that to this verse; Chrysostom rejected it: 'Some say Paul here exhorts his own wife; but it is not so, but some other woman, or the husband of one of them'. The person is unknown.

p: A co-worker in Philippi. Eusebius identified him with Clement, later leader of the church in Rome.
b: Clement (Latin Clemens) is a common Roman name, fitting a colony. Eusebius says that Paul, in his letter to the Philippians, 'informs us that this Clement was his fellow-worker', meaning Clement who led the church in Rome at the end of the first century (Church History 3.15). Philippians itself does not say which Clement is meant, and the name was common.

p: God's register of the living and the faithful, from Exodus to Revelation.
b: The picture is of a city register of citizens, God's list of those who belong to him. Moses prays to be wiped out 'from your book that you have written' (Exodus 32:32); the Psalms pray for the wicked to 'be wiped out of the scroll of life' (Psalm 69:28); Daniel speaks of 'everyone found written in the scroll' (Daniel 12:1); Jesus says 'your names stand written in heaven' (Luke 10:20); Revelation promises 'I will never erase his name from the book of life' (Revelation 3:5). For a church of colonists proud of their Roman enrollment, names written in heaven fit 3:20.
r: Exodus 32:32; Psalm 69:28; Daniel 12:1; Malachi 3:16; Luke 10:20; Revelation 3:5; 3:20

a: Rejoice in the Lord at all times
p: Joy here is a command, given by a prisoner to a church under pressure.
b: The repeated command (see 3:1) is not 'be happy about everything'. It is 'rejoice in the Lord': the reason for joy lies in who the Lord is and what he has done, which circumstances do not change. Paul writes it in chains, after naming quarrels and opponents. 'Again I will say it' shows he expects them to find it hard. Compare 1 Thessalonians 5:16, written to the church in Thessalonica, farther along the same road.

t: The Lord is near: in time or in place?
p: Either Christ's coming is soon, or the Lord is close at hand to those who call on him.
b: Ho kyrios engys can mean 'the Lord's coming is near' (as in 3:20 and 'Maranatha', 1 Corinthians 16:22) or 'the Lord is close by', as Psalm 145:18 says: 'Near is the LORD to everyone who calls to him' (Psalm 145:18). The next verse, about prayer, fits the second; the call to gentleness fits the first. Paul may intend both.

p: The same verb as Jesus' 'stop worrying' in the Sermon on the Mount.
b: Merimnao 'worry, be anxious' is Jesus' word in Matthew 6:25: 'stop worrying about your life'. Paul uses the same verb positively in 2:20 for Timothy, who will 'worry about your affairs'. So the command is not to stop caring; it is to turn worry into prayer, with thanks. The four words for prayer (prayer, pleading, thanks, requests) cover every kind of asking.

p: Phroureo: to guard, keep under guard, like a garrison.
b: Phroureo means to guard or keep under guard; in 2 Corinthians 11:32 a governor 'guarded' the city of Damascus. In a city with Roman soldiers and veterans the picture would be familiar: God's peace as the garrison posted over their hearts and thoughts. The peace is 'greater than anything the mind can reach', nous, which may mean it is beyond understanding, or that it achieves more than any human planning can.

p: Paul uses the moral words of his Greek neighbors, including arete, 'virtue'.
b: Several of these words are common in Greek moral writing and rare in Paul: arete 'virtue, excellence' appears only here in his letters, and euphema 'well spoken of' and prosphile 'pleasing' are found nowhere else in the New Testament. Paul tells the church to recognize what is good wherever it is found, and 'keep thinking these over' (logizesthe, reckon, take into account). Readers have used the verse to support learning from the best of non-Christian culture; others note that 4:9 immediately ties the list to what they saw in Paul.

p: Anathallo is a gardening word: to sprout or flower again.
b: Anethalete, 'you bloomed again', pictures a plant flowering again after a dry season. Paul is careful not to sound as if they had forgotten him: 'You were thinking of me all along, but the right moment never came'. Readers have noted that this thank-you comes late in the letter and is very guarded. Some see a sign that it was a separate note (see 3:1); others see tact, since in the ancient world thanks for a gift could imply a debt of a client to a patron, and Paul avoids putting himself under obligation.

p: A word of the philosophers: self-sufficient. Paul's sufficiency lies in Christ (4:13).
b: Autarkes in philosophy meant self-sufficient, independent of circumstances, a quality Stoic and Cynic teachers praised; in ordinary use it meant simply 'having enough, content' (the lexicons give both). Paul uses the word his Greek readers knew, then changes its center: not 'I am enough for myself', but 'I have strength for everything in the one who makes me strong' (4:13).

a: I have been let into the secret
p: Myeo is the word for initiation into the mystery religions.
b: Memyemai 'I have been initiated' is the verb used of being admitted into the secret rites of mystery cults (the lexicons note this as its chief classical use). Paul uses it with a smile: the secret he has been let into is how to have plenty and how to go without. 'Live low' is the tapeinoo word again (see 2:3, 2:8).

p: Often quoted for sports and success. In context it is about enduring hunger and want.
b: The verse is printed on sports gear and quoted before big games and exams. In its setting, 'everything' means the situations of 4:12: plenty and hunger, having and going without. Paul is saying that in Christ he can endure any circumstance, not that Christ guarantees any achievement. Readers are not wrong to find strength here for hard tasks; they misread it if it becomes a promise of success. The Greek panta ischyo is 'I am strong for all things'. See the variant on 'the one'.

t: An account of giving and receiving
p: Business language: an account with credits and debits. Only Philippi entered into it with Paul.
b: Eis logon doseos kai lempseos is bookkeeping language, 'a matter of giving and receiving'. Paul usually refused support from a church while working there (1 Corinthians 9:12-15; 2 Corinthians 11:7-9), but he accepted it from Philippi, even while he was in Thessalonica (4:16) and later in Corinth: 'The brothers who came from Macedonia fully supplied what I lacked' (2 Corinthians 11:9). Philippi stands out as a partner (see 1:5). The bookkeeping goes on in 4:17-18: the 'fruit that keeps adding up in your account' (eis logon hymon) is credit that is theirs, not Paul's, as Jesus speaks of treasure stored in heaven (Matthew 6:20); and 'I have been paid in full' (apecho panta) is the wording of a receipt, the verb Jesus uses of hypocrites who 'are already paid in full' (Matthew 6:2). Readers who stress grace read the 'account' as God's generous reward, not a payment earned.

p: After Philippi, Paul went on through Amphipolis and Apollonia to Thessalonica (Acts 17:1).
b: After leaving Philippi, Paul and his companions traveled through Amphipolis and Apollonia to Thessalonica (Acts 17:1). The Philippians sent help there 'once and then a second time', soon after the church was founded. In 1 Thessalonians 2:9 Paul says he worked night and day there so as not to be a burden, which suggests the gifts did not cover everything.

t: A soothing smell, an acceptable sacrifice
p: The Old Testament phrase for sacrifices that please God, now used of a gift of money.
b: Osme euodias is the Greek Old Testament's phrase for an offering's smell that pleases God: 'The LORD smelled the soothing smell' (Genesis 8:21), and the regular sacrifices in Numbers 15 and 28. Ephesians 5:2 uses it of Christ's self-offering. Paul turns the church's gift to a prisoner into temple worship: 'a sacrifice that God accepts' (compare 2:17).
r: Genesis 8:21; Exodus 29:18; Numbers 15:10; Ephesians 5:2; Romans 12:1; Hebrews 13:16

a: my God will fill every need you have
p: A promise to a giving church. Readers differ on how far it reaches.
b: The verb is the same as 'I am filled up' in 4:18: you filled my need, my God will fill yours. The promise is given to people who had given beyond their means (2 Corinthians 8:1-3 describes the Macedonian churches' generosity in poverty). The verse is sometimes read as a promise of material wealth; the setting points another way: 'every need' stands beside 4:11-13, where Paul has learned to go without, and 'in glory, in Christ Jesus' as the measure and place of the supply.

p: Not the emperor's family, but the slaves and freed slaves who served the emperor.
b: Hoi ek tes Kaisaros oikias are 'those of Caesar's household': in Roman usage the emperor's household included the many slaves and former slaves who ran his palace and his offices, in Rome and in the provinces. So the phrase does not mean that the emperor's relatives had become believers. The phrase was used of the imperial service at Rome but also in the provinces, so it does not settle where Paul was held. Michael Flexsenhar (Christians in Caesar's Household, 2019) has argued that the imperial slaves Paul means were in Asia Minor. It shows the good news reaching people close to the center of power, and a colony proud of Rome would notice.

a: May the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ
p: A Semitic way of saying 'with you'. The same blessing closes Galatians and Philemon.
b: 'With your spirit' means with you, the whole person, spoken to the inner life. The same ending closes Galatians 6:18 and Philemon 25. The Byzantine text and the KJV read 'with you all. Amen' (see the variant). The letter that began with 'grace to you' (1:2) ends with grace.
